claims.label: About a tenth of a flora's seeds could survive sea-drift across 900 miles
claims.statement: Based on flotation and germination experiments, the seeds of roughly 10 per cent of the plants of a flora, after drying, could be floated by sea currents across about 900 miles of sea and still germinate.

operationalizations.text: Compile experimental seed buoyancy duration and saltwater germination survival data across regional floras, combined with surface ocean current drift velocities (~1-3 knots), to calculate the proportion of species whose dried seeds can remain afloat and viable for the time required to drift 900 miles (~20-40 days).

Compile published seawater flotation-duration and post-immersion germination experiments for a representative flora, combine survival time with current velocities, and estimate the fraction capable of 900-mile dispersal. Confidence intervals excluding 10 percent would refute Darwin's numerical estimate.

Estimate the fraction of species in a regional flora whose dried seeds stay buoyant and then germinate after a seawater exposure long enough to cross about 900 miles. A flora-scale fraction far from one tenth, under that protocol, would refute the numerical claim.

obstacles: Standardized saltwater immersion and flotation durations for dried seeds across entire non-coastal floras are only compiled for subsets of species in trait databases and scattered experimental papers.
No known unified dataset samples a representative whole flora.
Ocean travel time depends strongly on route and seed state.
Published experiments may overrepresent dispersal-prone taxa.
No public dataset applies one seawater flotation and germination protocol to a whole flora.
Available buoyancy trials often use fresh water and omit germination after drying.
Transit time for 900 miles depends on a current speed the claim leaves implicit.

claims.label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
claims.statement: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.

operationalizations.text: Measure phenotypic selection gradients (regressions of relative survival and reproductive success on heritable trait values) across wild populations; non-zero directional and stabilizing selection gradients confirm that advantageous variations are preserved and injurious ones eliminated.

Estimate associations between heritable trait or allele values and survival and reproductive success across populations. Consistently positive selection differentials for advantageous variants and negative differentials for harmful variants support the mechanism; absent or reversed fitness effects refute it in tested systems.

Estimate the distribution of fitness effects from allele-frequency spectra, and estimate surplus offspring from life tables. Purifying selection would be confirmed if deleterious alleles are systematically rarer than neutral alleles and if populations produce far more offspring than survive; the differential-success clause would be refuted if fitness effects did not predict frequency change. The sentence that names this process natural selection has no separate measurement.

obstacles: Part of the statement defines the term 'Natural Selection', while the empirical component requires separating genetic covariance from environmental covariance between traits and fitness.
Available selection gradient compilations are biased toward short-term studies of terrestrial vertebrates, insects, and annual plants.
Advantage is environment-dependent and risks being defined circularly by survival.
Available longitudinal fitness data cover a small fraction of organisms.
An advantage defined as higher survival or reproduction makes the central clause close to a definition of fitness.
Population-genomic samples are concentrated in humans and model organisms.
Life tables show excess births without identifying which heritable differences selection retains.

claims.label: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution
claims.statement: Fear of humans is slowly acquired by animal populations persecuted by man, so animals on uninhabited islands are tame and heavily hunted large birds are wilder than small ones.

operationalizations.text: Regress flight initiation distance (FID, the distance at which an animal flees an approaching human) against island vs. mainland status, time since human colonization/persecution intensity, and body mass across bird and reptile species, controlling for phylogeny.

Relate flight-initiation distance or approach tolerance across populations to quantified duration and intensity of human persecution, controlling for body size, urbanization, and phylogeny. Increasing fear with exposure supports the claim.

Regress flight-initiation distance on island isolation, history of human presence, hunting pressure, and body size. Longer distances where persecution has been longer or more intense, and shorter distances on uninhabited islands, would support the claim; no such pattern, or a pattern explained by predator fauna alone, would count against it.

obstacles: Observational FID measurements reflect both evolved genetic wariness and within-lifetime learning/habituation to benign vs. hunting human presence.
Flight-initiation measurements are scattered rather than centrally standardized.
Urban habituation and species sorting confound persecution history.
Flight distance confounds evolved fear, individual learning, habitat, and the background predator community.
The compilations are snapshots, so they do not measure the word 'slowly'.
Geographic bias toward Europe, North America, and Australia leaves many persecution histories unsampled.

claims.label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
claims.statement: Because more individuals of each species are born than can survive, there is a recurring struggle for existence, so any individual that varies even slightly in a way profitable to itself has a better chance of surviving and thus of being naturally selected.

operationalizations.text: Estimate reproductive output relative to carrying capacity (juvenile mortality rates) alongside standardized phenotypic selection gradients (Lande-Arnold beta and survival differentials) across wild populations; confirm if net fecundity routinely exceeds replacement and phenotypic variants consistently experience non-zero survival differentials.

Estimate lifetime reproductive success or survival as a function of a measured heritable trait under density limitation. A consistently positive selection differential for profitable variants, coupled with excess offspring mortality, supports the claim; no differential refutes it in each tested population.

Estimate low-density population growth and the surplus of births over replacement from matrix models and fecundity schedules, then ask whether small heritable advantages predict higher survival or reproductive success in the same populations. Persistent geometric potential with realized populations held far below it would support the overproduction premise; a general failure of slight heritable differences to predict fitness would challenge the selection step only if 'profitable' is defined independently of the fitness outcome.

obstacles: Longitudinal individual-level survival and trait data are heavily biased toward vertebrates and short-lived herbaceous plants.
Unmeasured environmental covariates (e.g., nutritional state) can create non-causal correlations between traits and survival.
Heritability and fitness are rarely measured together.
Results from monitored species cannot establish universality.
A variation that is profitable to its bearer is already defined by improved survival or reproduction, so that half of the statement is nearly analytic.
Public demographic databases rarely pair individual-level heritable differences with fitness in the same rows.
Density dependence, measurement of 'slight' variation, and publication bias in selection studies all change the apparent strength of the result.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: Older members of distinct groups differ less from each other than living members
claims.statement: Groups that have changed much over known geological periods should, in older formations, approach each other slightly, so that their older members differ from each other in fewer characters than their living members do.

operationalizations.text: For pairs of sister higher taxa (e.g., birds and crocodilians, mammals and reptiles), compute pairwise morphological character differences between their Paleozoic/Mesozoic members and compare them to the character differences between their extant members.

For pairs of related higher groups, compare morphological distance between older fossil members and between extant members using homologous characters. Support requires smaller between-group distance in older strata specifically for groups with substantial later modification.

For pairs of groups with a long later history, compare character distances among their early members with distances among their living members. Early members as distinct as living members, or more so, would refute a backward approach between the groups.

obstacles: Fossil incompleteness means older taxa have more missing character states, requiring distance metrics normalized for observable characters.
Suitable shared-character matrices exist for limited clades.
Early members can be mosaics without being mutually closer overall.
Suitable matrices exist for a minority of the group pairs in the scope.
Loss of soft tissues can make older fossils look more alike than the living animals were.

claims.label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
claims.statement: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.

operationalizations.text: Test for reciprocal phenotypic selection gradients and correlated geographic/phylogenetic trait matching between floral tube/spur dimensions and insect pollinator proboscis lengths across populations and sister taxa.

Map floral and pollinator structural traits, interaction effectiveness and phylogenies, then test reciprocal trait matching and correlated evolutionary change. Reciprocal fitness benefits and repeated correlated shifts support mutual adaptation; matching explained solely by shared environment or one-sided adaptation weakens it.

Match floral measurements to the morphology of recorded insect visitors and test whether changes on the two phylogenies are correlated. Trait matching beyond a null of random visits would support mutual modification; matching explained entirely by pollinators filtering flowers that already fit would refute reciprocal adaptation. Simultaneous versus sequential change is a further, weaker contrast using relative timing on time-calibrated trees.

obstacles: Comparative trait matching alone cannot easily distinguish simultaneous reciprocal coevolution from sequential unilateral tracking ('one after the other') where one partner adapts to a pre-existing trait of the other.
Reciprocal fitness measurements on both the plant and the insect partner in the same populations are available for only a handful of model systems.
Interaction databases rarely include reciprocal fitness effects or fine structural measurements.
Trait matching can result from ecological filtering rather than coevolution.
Visitor morphology and corolla measurements are only partly in the same databases as interactions.
One-sided adaptation and ecological filtering produce trait matching without reciprocal change.
Network coverage is strong for a few floras and poor for most insect-plant pairs.

claims.label: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts
claims.statement: Closely allied but distinct species living in distant parts of the world under different conditions often retain nearly the same instincts, which is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor.

operationalizations.text: Quantify phylogenetic signal (Pagel's $\lambda$ or Blomberg's $K$) in innate behavioral traits (e.g., nest construction type, foraging stratum, song structure) across congeneric or confamilial bird species inhabiting different biogeographic realms and climatic niches, controlling for environmental distance.

Quantify behavioural similarity among close relatives occupying different environments and compare phylogenetic versus environmental effects. Strong behavioural phylogenetic signal after environmental control supports inherited instinct.

Compare behavioral similarity of sister species that live in distant regions with the ecological distance between those regions. High similarity of nest, migration, or foraging habits despite different conditions supports retention from a common ancestor; behavior tracking local conditions rather than relatedness would count against it.

obstacles: Some behavioral similarities across distant regions could reflect retention of ancestral habitat preferences (niche conservatism) in addition to purely environment-independent behavioral inheritance.
Many instincts lack standardized cross-species measurements.
Similar unmeasured ecological pressures can mimic inheritance.
Foraging traits and tracks are proxies; nest, song, and display instincts are mostly uncoded.
Similar behavior can be shared selection in unmeasured niches rather than inheritance.
Thrushes and wrens illustrate a claim stated for allied animals generally.

claims.label: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate
claims.statement: Species in nature are limited in their geographic ranges by competition with other organisms at least as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.

operationalizations.text: Synthesize experimental transplant studies across range boundaries (warm/equatorial/low-elevation edges vs cold/polar/high-elevation edges) that factorially manipulate biotic interactions (competitor/predator exclusion) and climate, and compare the frequency and magnitude of biotic versus climatic range limitation.

Partition explained variation in range limits between climate and biotic-interaction predictors across many species, supplemented by transplants or invasions beyond native boundaries. A median biotic contribution at least as large as climate supports the claim.

Classify range boundaries as coinciding with physiological climate limits or as lying inside those limits where interacting species turn over, then compare the two frequencies. The claim would be confirmed if biotic boundaries are at least as common as climatic ones; it would be refuted if most boundaries match tolerance limits and competitor turnover adds no explanatory power.

obstacles: Observational species distribution models (SDMs) are heavily confounded by spatial autocorrelation between climate and competitor distributions, requiring experimental transplant datasets which exist for only several hundred species.
Biotic limitation often includes predation, herbivory, and parasitism in addition to strict interspecific competition.
Climate and competitors covary spatially.
Interaction databases omit many weak, local or context-dependent interactions.
Tolerance data exist for a minority of species, so many boundaries cannot be classified.
Species turnover at an edge is a proxy for competition, not a demonstration of it.
Dispersal limitation produces interior edges that look biotic.

claims.label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
claims.statement: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.

operationalizations.text: Test whether competition coefficients in experimental communities and extinction probabilities during biological invasions or clade replacements are negatively correlated with phylogenetic distance (i.e. congeneric or closely related species suffer stronger competitive suppression or higher local extirpation).

For invasions, radiations and replacement events, test whether decline or extinction risk rises with phylogenetic and niche similarity to the expanding form. Disproportionate losses among nearest relatives support the prediction; losses unrelated or negatively related to kinship refute it.

When a form expands or a non-native species establishes, compare the decline of closest relatives with the decline of distant co-occurring taxa, in fossils and in modern assemblages. Greater impact on sister lineages would confirm the claim; impact that is independent of relatedness, or stronger on distant natives, would refute it.

obstacles: Close relatives share similar environmental tolerances (habitat filtering), which creates positive co-occurrence patterns in observational data that can mask competitive exclusion.
Tracking competitive extermination specifically 'during the progress of formation' of an incipient variety in the wild is rarely captured in standard datasets.
Close relatives may facilitate one another or differ ecologically despite kinship.
Direct observations of speciation coincident with competitor extinction are rare.
Co-occurrence and replacement are not direct measures of competition.
Invasions often hit naive distant taxa harder than close relatives, which cuts against a simple test.
Fossil sister-species pairs are rarely resolved.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent
claims.statement: Because the embryo is the animal in a less modified state that partly reveals the structure of its progenitor, two groups that pass through the same or similar embryonic stages are descended from the same or similar parents, however different their adults; this is why embryonic characters are the most valuable for classification.

operationalizations.text: In clades where adults are highly modified by parasitism or sessility (e.g. Cirripedia, Rhizocephala, Tunicata, parasitic copepods), compare phylogenetic trees built from embryonic/larval morphological characters versus adult characters against independent genomic phylogenies.

Quantify embryonic character similarity among animal groups and test whether it predicts independently inferred molecular common ancestry and improves classification relative to adult convergence-prone characters. Agreement supports embryonic structure as evidence of descent.

Compare trees or distance matrices built from embryonic characters with independent molecular trees, and compare both with trees built from adult characters. The claim is confirmed if groups that share embryonic stages are clades on the molecular tree more reliably than adult similarity would indicate, and refuted if embryonic similarity groups species that molecular data place far apart.

obstacles: Secondary loss of larval stages (direct development) or convergent larval adaptations (e.g. planktotrophic larval convergence) can occasionally confound larval-only trees.
Embryonic datasets are strongly biased toward model species.
Developmental similarity may reflect constraint as well as ancestry.
Using embryonic similarity both to classify a group and to prove its common descent is circular unless the tree is molecular.
The most conserved developmental stage is often mid-embryogenesis rather than the earliest embryo, so 'the embryo' is not a single comparable object.
Comparative embryology matrices exist for scattered groups, not for animal groups in general.
